devpost_page.title: DocSpot
devpost_page.tagline: An all-in-one platform for physicians to find specialists and send referrals, making connections between physicians faster and more trusted.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Imagine you’re a physician whose patient needs a specialist. Finding the right person can be difficult, especially when many physicians are digitally dark or hard to reach through the usual industry channels. We wanted to hear directly from an HCP, so we reached out to Dr. Justin Strickland, the owner of a pharmaceutical practice here in Atlanta. He told us, “ Even some of our local physicians who we have known and worked with for years have become increasingly difficult to reach after their practices were acquired. ” Today, 82% of U.S. physicians work for hospitals or corporate entities ( PAI/Avalere ). And in rural areas, finding a doctor can be even harder, as urban areas have nearly three times as many physicians per 100,000 people ( AAMC, 2022 ). To bridge this gap, we looked at how physicians learn about new critical clinical tools and found that professional relationships play an important role. In a survey, 76.4% of physicians named other physicians among their most trusted sources of health information ( Kruger et al., 2012 ). That’s where DocSpot comes in. Built on Impiricus' network of over 1 million opted-in healthcare professionals, DocSpot maps national physician connections so doctors can refer patients, ask clinical questions, and surface telehealth or trial opportunities.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: DocSpot connects physicians based on specialty, experience, and clinical needs, creating a network that introduces more HCPs to Impiricus’ services. An HCP can find a specialist for a referral, explore telehealth and clinical trial options, or find a colleague to answer a clinical question. Drawing from a comprehensive database of physicians and specialists across the US, DocSpot recommends relevant physicians, including those who have not joined Impiricus. For referrals, DocSpot ranks specialists by factors such as specialty, distance, and their relationship to the sender. It then drafts an editable electronic fax (e-fax) with limited patient information. The HCP reviews the recipient, draft, and privacy check before approving it, then tracks the request and response in one place through the platform. A physician outside Impiricus can respond without joining. After that first useful interaction, they can choose to connect with the sender on Impiricus and discover its services through a professional relationship.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Frontend: HTML, CSS, and plain JavaScript power the workflow. SVG draws the network map and groups physicians by specialty, while client-side code generates QR codes for fax previews. Backend and AI: Python FastAPI and Pydantic validate requests. The backend sends limited, structured details to OpenAI’s gpt-4.1-mini model to draft faxes and assist with privacy review. Physician data: We cleaned NPI Registry records in a Jupyter notebook and mapped taxonomy descriptions to DocSpot’s specialties. Consent and email: After a specialist accepts, the referring physician reviews a consent form. FastAPI serves the signing page, and the Resend Email API sends the patient a link. The patient confirms their date of birth and signs before DocSpot shares further details.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Our first visual network map consisted of singular, unrelated nodes, and eventually became difficult to read as we added physicians and their connections. To address this challenge, we separated clinicians into specialty groups, made the nodes easier to distinguish, and added a list view. NPI records also used different descriptions for similar specialties, so we had to clean and map those labels before using the records in recommendations. Referrals also required careful handling of patient information. The sending physician reviews the request before it goes out. If the receiving physician accepts, the patient signs a consent form before DocSpot shares any further patient details.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we’re proud of
sections.text: This was everyone on our team’s first hackathon, so we’re proud we turned a physician’s experience into a working prototype under a tight deadline. We're also proud of the network map, which gives HCPs a visual way to see where care is available, and most importantly, helps improve patient care.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Building a healthcare product taught us how much goes into a physician’s decision to contact a colleague. They need to find the right person, protect the patient’s privacy, and review what they send. Because those decisions can affect a real patient’s care, we learned to look at each step from the physician’s perspective and make DocSpot useful in their day-to-day work.

sections.heading: What’s next for DocSpot
sections.text: We hope to explore partnerships with Careset, HealthVerity, or Symphony Health, and GaHIN to improve our physician and relationship data. We also want to integrate a secure e-fax service so HCPs can send and track real requests. We would start with a pilot in one rural Georgia county, learn how local HCPs find specialists and respond to referrals, adjust DocSpot based on their feedback, and then expand to other communities.

devpost_page.title: IronBook
devpost_page.tagline: A new way for manufacturers to learn.

sections.text: Ironbook Preserve the knowledge of every expert on your shop floor before they walk out the door.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: 11,000 Americans turn 65 every single day. By 2027, 4.1 million workers will hit retirement age, and nowhere is the damage more acute than manufacturing. Skilled machinists, technicians, and engineers carry decades of irreplaceable knowledge: why a machine sounds different when a bearing is failing, which tooling setup works for a specific aluminum alloy, where the oil fill port hides on a 30-year-old press. A recent survey found that 57% of retiring Baby Boomers have shared less than half the knowledge needed to do their job and 21% have shared none of it. That knowledge walks out the door with them, permanently. Passing it on the old way doesn't scale. A typical apprenticeship takes 4–5 years . Meanwhile, 584,000 manufacturing jobs sat unfilled in January 2024 alone. We built Ironbook to close that gap, not with manuals or videos, but with a living, queryable 3D model of the physical world , paired with an AI agent that can navigate it in real time.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Take your phone, walk around a machine, a part, or a workstation, and photograph it from multiple angles. Ironbook reconstructs a photorealistic 3D Gaussian splat and pairs it with an AI agent that can navigate that scene in real time . Instead of a static photo or a flat PDF manual, a new technician can: Ask natural questions — "What's that valve on the left side?" or "Show me the oil fill port." Let the agent navigate — the AI physically flies the camera through the 3D scene, zooms in, and highlights the object on screen Speak instead of type — voice input keeps hands free on the shop floor Build a living library — every scanned asset becomes a searchable, queryable record of institutional knowledge The AI doesn't just describe where to look. It goes there , moving the camera through the scene spatially to answer the question in context.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: Capture Users upload 20+ overlapping photos of any object or space. The app provides a coverage score and warns about gaps in coverage. Reconstruct: a 3-tier pipeline with no dead ends COLMAP runs structure-from-motion to recover precise camera poses and a sparse point cloud msplat — a Metal-accelerated 3DGS trainer — optimizes tens of thousands of 3D Gaussians on the Apple GPU, hitting **~24 dB PSNR on M-series chips MLX fallback handles CPU-only machines when Metal isn't available Depth-anything ONNX fallback uses monocular depth estimation for a navigable 2.5D reconstruction when no GPU pipeline is present You always get something you can explore. Query: an AI agent that acts, not just describes An AI agent backed by Claude (vision + structured output) receives the user's message, a live screenshot of the current 3D camera view, and the current camera state. It returns: A natural-language answer A sequence of camera actions the frontend executes: fly_to , look_at , highlight , rotate , zoom , move , reset_view , and more The agent is connected to the viewer via an MCP-style action protocol, structured JSON that the frontend interprets and executes in real time as the conversation unfolds. Render: a WebGL2 renderer built from scratch A custom WebGL2 Gaussian splat renderer supports orbit, walk, and fly camera modes with WASD + mouse. It executes agent actions live, frame by frame, as the user asks questions. Stack Layer Technology Frontend React 18, Vite, TypeScript, custom

sections.heading: Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Getting real-time navigation to feel spatial. The core insight of Ironbook is that the AI doesn't describe the answer — it shows you. Designing the action protocol and getting smooth camera animation to execute agent instructions frame-by-frame required careful engineering on both the agent output schema and the WebGL renderer's animation loop. Building a robust reconstruction pipeline. Real shop floors don't have studio lighting or perfectly overlapping photos. We built a 3-tier fallback system so the app produces something useful whether you have Apple Silicon and Metal tooling or just a CPU — while being transparent about which backend is running via a /api/health endpoint. Grounding the AI in 3D space. Claude receives a screenshot of the current camera view as context. Getting it to reason correctly about spatial relationships (distinguishing left from right, near from far, what's occluded) required careful prompt engineering and structured output validation. The agent must reason about the scene in camera-space coordinates, not abstract space. Handling HEIC from iPhones. Most shop floor photos come from iPhones. We added pillow-heif to transparently convert HEIC to compatible formats before they enter the pipeline, so users never have to think about file formats.

sections.heading: Accomplishments We're Proud Of
sections.text: A custom WebGL2 Gaussian splat renderer built entirely from scratch, with orbit, walk, and fly modes, and real-time agent-driven camera control An agent action protocol that turns Claude's structured JSON output into live 3D navigation — not just chat, but spatial exploration A 3-tier reconstruction fallback so the app works on any machine, not just GPU-equipped workstations 77 tests across backend (27) and frontend (50), plus full TypeScript strict-mode coverage A full observability stack (Sentry + Langfuse) for monitoring AI performance and errors in production

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: The hardest part of AI spatial navigation isn't the AI: it's the interface between language and geometry. Getting the model to express camera intent in a way the renderer can faithfully execute required treating the output schema as an API contract, not a suggestion. Structured output validation was essential. We also learned that degradation matters more than perfection. A rough 2.5D scene that you can query is infinitely more useful than a failed reconstruction. Every decision in the pipeline was shaped by the question: what does the user get if this step fails?

sections.heading: What's Next for Ironbook
sections.text: Multi-user shared scene libraries — a team-wide knowledge base where every scanned asset is searchable Video upload → automatic frame extraction — capture a wal

devpost_page.title: Logicverse
devpost_page.tagline: Reality exists in the human mind, and nowhere else. This experiment harvests humanoids and their associated data, cleansing their sinful nature into a purely formal representation.

sections.text: Welcome to the Logicverse. We wanted to make a simulation of humanity, in the online era. It works almost completely deterministically (aside from some small frontend ML to associate faces with people in our knowledge base).

sections.heading: Analytical conversationalist
sections.text: We scraped a bunch of data from the HN discord, GitHub, LinkedIn (we got banned 4 times), Devpost about the interests, likes, projects, histories, and more of our fellow hackers. Then from this we built up a huge knowledge-base of ~90,000 relational facts in a logic programming language to derive conversation (which is I think how humans do conversation too). Conversation is defined purely logically. For example, this query identifies a possible topic of conversation between two interlocutors who recently "did a similar activity". This is indicated by the <didRecently> relation. The knowledge-base engine can run dozens of these queries against tens of thousands of facts and figure out possible dialogue. SELECT ?cmd WHERE { GRAPH <metaverse/graph/scene> { ?A <is> <present> . ?B <is> <present> . ?A <alias> ?aliasA . ?B <alias> ?aliasB . } ?A <didRecently> ?activity . ?B <didRecently> ?activity . ?activity <name> ?activityName . FILTER (?A != ?B) BIND (CONCAT( ?aliasA, " (to ", ?aliasB, "): Have you been doing ", ?activityName, " lately? So have I!\n\n", ?aliasB, ": Great minds." ) as ?cmd) } Sometimes people will have very little in common, in which case we encode topics of possible smalltalk, and in the extreme case, topics that an individual may talk or think about with themselves.

sections.heading: Formal speech
sections.text: The dialogues are presented as scripts in a custom domain specific language that we designed. [Zac wearing short long wig, costume XY3P ] [Amber wearing blonde long wig, costume AG0R , ginger beard] [enter Zac from stage left] Zac: I think, therefore I am. Zac (thinking): Only every time we meet. These dialogues are chosen from a selection presented deterministically by our librettist (a Rust module), and sent to the renderer to be realised in the real world. The renderer interprets these stage directions line by line just as humans would.

sections.heading: Who's there?
sections.text: When a human sits down in front of our TV, our system knows. It figures out who has appeared, and creates a virtual alter-ego of them within the screen. These are the subjects and the objects of our facts and relations, and of the conversations to be had with the other inhabitants.

sections.heading: Tech
sections.text: We wrote the project in pretty much all Rust--taking a fairly low level approach to the graphics with Bevy--plus a little Python for some web scraping. The knowledge-base is built with the amazing SPARQL query language against RDL Turtle data.

sections.heading: Scraping
sections.text: We wrote scrapers for Discord, Github, and Devpost. Discord was the hardest because we had no admin access. Instead we automated the browser, scripting the clicks that open each member’s full profile and reading the HTML. GitHub and Devpost were easier, since both expose their data in a structured form. Devpost was especially useful because many people list their full names. We use those names in the display and in the script language. We also linked the profiles with relations such as “collaborates with” and “follows”, and with identity links that connect one person’s accounts across platforms.

devpost_page.tagline: Bubu is a financial education game for middle school to college students, covering saving, budgeting, and credit through interactive lessons and real-life scenarios with Bubu, your learning buddy.

sections.text: Bubu-Dins Before the lease, the loan, or the first paycheck, try the decision while it still costs thinking, not rent.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Most people learn about money the expensive way: a lease they barely understood, a card that felt free until it wasn't, a loan payment that arrived before the paycheck felt real. We wanted a rehearsal first. Walk into a world, try the choice, then say why . Not a chatbot that picks a product for you.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Bubu is a PathMX learning game. You sign in, keep your own progress, and move through a map. Learn → Try it → Review on housing, investing, and a personal-finance portfolio. Walk Storyworld , step into the Bank , and talk with Tram , a fictional banker who asks about tradeoffs instead of selling an account. Open a dashboard fed by Capital One’s Nessie teaching sandbox (read-only). Practice numbers never write to a real bank. Ask Dr.Bos for office-hours help by using Gemini API . Only you and the app save completion.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Lessons and character voices live in paths/ as ordinary Markdown. A TypeScript plugin adds the map, portfolio board, dashboard, bank scene, Nessie route, and tutors. Dr.Bos and Tram run server-side with keys in .env , never in the browser. Nessie is GET-only. Tests keep sandbox data, fictional cash, and learning credit from collapsing into one fake wallet.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Keeping three kinds of money honest: Nessie balances, Bank-scene practice cash, and Bubu learning credit. Keeping AI in its lane: no advice, no “you passed,” no invented rates, still a voice you would actually ask.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: A full loop: sign in, try a choice, refresh, progress is still there. A Bank you can stand in. A portfolio board with real stops. Dr.Bos who can teach and cannot grade. Sponsor sandbox data used read-only, with tests so the key never leaks to the browser.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: The hard design is who is allowed to say the work is done. Sandbox APIs are gold as evidence to think with, and a trap if you dress them up as the learner’s real bank. If the lesson is Markdown, the team can change the course without rewriting the engine.

devpost_page.tagline: WiSPR is a wearable badge that detects hazards and enables silent team alerts through vibrations, LEDs, and a ticket tracker, turning invisible risks into clear and actionable safety signals.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: As a technician, you often have to work long hours in harsh and noise-polluted environments. Communication becomes difficult, and detecting danger isn’t always possible when machinery and environmental sounds blur together. In these conditions, even small lapses in awareness can lead to serious risks. Our team wanted to create a safety solution that doesn’t depend on sound or visibility. That’s where our idea for WiSPR, or a Wireless Safety Pulse Relay system, began. We were inspired by the need for clear, reliable communication in the moments when it matters most.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: In noisy or hazardous environments, technicians often face risks they can’t see or hear. WiSPR is a wearable badge that keeps you safe, whether you’re working alone or with a teammate. When you’re working solo, WiSPR uses a humidity and temperature sensor to detect dangerous conditions. If it senses risk, the badge vibrates, flashes an LED, and displays a warning. This gives you a subtle, immediate alert before danger strikes. When you’re working with a teammate, WiSPR becomes a silent communication system. Press the button, and your teammate’s badge responds with a unique vibration and LED pattern, letting them know if you’re okay, need help, or are in danger, all without a single word spoken. Every signal matters. Every pulse keeps you and your team safe. WiSPR transforms invisible risks into tactile and visual alerts. Coupled with a seamless ticket tracker interface, WiSPR ensures safety isn’t just an idea; it’s in every signal.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: WiSPR was built using simple and affordable components to create a wearable safety system. At the core is an Arduino, which reads data from a DHT11 sensor to monitor temperature and humidity. An LCD screen displays the current readings, while LEDs and a buzzer provide visual and audio alerts for hazards or help requests. A button allows the wearer to send alerts, with short presses signaling assistance and long presses signaling hazards. The system also uses TX and RX pins to communicate between Arduinos, enabling teammates to receive alerts in real time. All hardware components were connected on a breadboard, and the software was programmed to automatically manage sensor readings, button inputs, alerts, and inter-device communication, making the system reliable, responsive, and ready for future expansions. Our team then worked on the design and front-end development of the WiSPR dashboard. This is the interface technicians would actually see in the field, via their laptops. We started with Figma, keeping it clean and easy to understand at a glance. Our main theme color is blue, which represents safety, clarity, and trust which ties into WiSPR’s role as a reliable communication system. Then, we used red and blue for the alerts, which are common color logics. We then built the dashboard in React, inside VS Code, using custom CSS to match the Figma design exactly. It updates live using simulated data for temperature and humidity, and automatically switches between Safe, Warning

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: Wiring multiple components on the breadboard was tricky, and loose connections often caused unexpected issues. Buttons occasionally misbehaved when pressed too quickly, and managing the timing for LEDs, buzzers, and the LCD display required precision to ensure no alerts were missed. Establishing reliable communication between Arduinos was also essential to prevent false alerts and ensure accurate status updates on the LCD. During the creation of the AutoCAD model, it was challenging to create proper extrusions and determine the right dimensions. We wanted the badge to be small enough to wear comfortably, yet large enough to hold all essential components such as the Arduino, sensors, and LEDs. Balancing functionality with wearability took multiple iterations and design adjustments. Learning Figma, React, and VS Code from scratch also came with a steep learning curve. We encountered frequent coding errors, and debugging was often a tedious process. However, with persistence and plenty of YouTube tutorials, we overcame these challenges and turned our ideas into a working product.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: We're proud of bringing WiSPR from concept to reality in a short amount of time, especially since the majority of our team are beginners. Our team successfully integrated hardware and software components, combining a temperature and humidity sensor, LEDs, and button controls to create a functional prototype that enhances safety through tactile and visual alerts. We’re also proud of designing a detailed 3D AutoCAD model that balanced ergonomics with internal space requirements, making the badge both wearable and practical. Alongside the hardware, we created a Figma prototype to visualize the user interface and designed a website using React, CSS, and JavaScript to showcase WiSPR’s ticketing system and functionality.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: Throughout the development of WiSPR, we learned how to interface DHT11 sensors with Arduino to measure temperature and humidity, and how to program LEDs and buzzers to create distinct alert patterns. We implemented short and long button presses to trigger different signals and established basic communication between two Arduinos for team-based alerts. We also learned to use an LCD display to show real-time data and system status while managing local and remote hazard logic separately. sections.text: AI-Powered Donor Discovery Donair uses Google Gemini AI with vector embeddings to semantically match your event description against a database of >110,000 historical publicly-available philanthropic donations sourced from CharityCAN and Indiana University. The system generates embeddings from your event description, then performs Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG) using vector similarity search in Supabase, along with web search for the latest results, to find recipients with aligned missions. From there, it identifies donors who have previously supported similar causes, filtering by capacity (gift size relative to your goal) and geographic relevance. devpost_page.title: GitFile
devpost_page.tagline: Git for ANY file type - Reducing storage costs by 500x, streamlining version control, and fostering efficient collaboration

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Git exists for programmers. We use it for coding. But what about documents with file types like PDFs, DOCX, XLSX, JPG, etc? Businesses today store backups of most their data on a repeating basis where the data doesn't change much every day, yet multiple copies are kept. As you might have guessed, every single copy only doubles the data being stored. The storage, bandwidth, and latency costs as a result of this are tremendous.

sections.heading: What It Does
sections.text: Our website is a fully-functional POC demonstrating how our custom-built git wrapper can transform the realm of unstructured data file types. When a user edits a pdf document or any other flat file, our software figures out the difference between the two versions and captures this. We offer an interface to edit a file and view the storage costs of having multiple versions after running a "git push" of the file to the cloud server. We effectively demonstrate the use of a low-level C wrapper surrounding git that works on flat files that have changes between versions.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built our frontend built in NextJS and hosted it on a Virtual Machine by using Terraform on an Azure ecosystem (also surrounded by other Azure services like gateways, networks, etc). We enlisted gitfile.tech as our root domain which hosts the main root of our website (as well as subdomains at main-server, ssh, etc for the other services that make the software work via A records using cloudfare setup). We connected an ssh session to a local git session to demo the functionality of git in an environment and the resulting version history in a dashboard one-screen format. In this system, we used Pinata to store our git history (similar to how GitHub acts as a cloud storage service) and made use of both storage and retrieval APIs effectively in this process. In our ssh terminal functionality at the bottom of the dashboard, we made use of Mozilla's PDF.js library for pdf-editing functionality which can be run with the command "edit " to edit the pdf and view its effects.

sections.heading: Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Setting up the low-level software which wrapped around common git functions like "git add" and "git push" to support our use case of flat filetypes was a bit challenging, but thanks to a bit of research we were able to get it done in time Getting the edit pdf functionality to work was a time consuming process as it required the need for multiple services to act appropriately and the documentation for this was very thorough and hard to finish understanding in a short period of hackathon time

sections.heading: Accomplishments We Are Proud of Us
sections.text: An accomplishment we are extremely proud of is the successful benchmarking of real-world business use cases to showcase the effectiveness of our solution. By applying our custom build wrapper we generated over a 500 times reduction in storage costs. This was pivotal in understanding the importance of something like this and the protentional value to business that rely on document storage. We are also really proud of completing in time! This hackathon we used a variety of technologies ranging from Azure hosting to integrating custom SSH functionalities which really pushed us to our limit. Finally being able to design a seamless user experience with functionalities like real time pdf editing and visualization in the dashboard was something we were really proud of considering we are not too experienced in front-end development,=.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: One major thing we learned was setting up SSH sessions restricted to specific holders and embedding it in an iframe on a static-rendered website taught us about the intricate workings of secure sessions and really opened our eyes to the importance of security in development. Using Terraform to deploy Azure services was another learning curve we had to tackle. We gained experience in infrastructure and understanding how to manage virtual machines, gateways, and networks in an Azure ecosystem. One of the most enriching aspects was writing custom commands in C that interfaced with Git's default commands. This dive into Got internals gave us all a better understanding of how version control systems work and how they can be modified for specific use cases.

sections.heading: What's Next for GitFile
sections.text: The next step would be to open source the project by sharing the code with the developer community and gather valuable feedback. By open sourcing developers and business can experiment with our tool and identify potential features or optimizations. We also want to look into ways to improve the editing and versioning features. This could be a refined dashboard interface or enhanced integration between the editing commands and version history visualization, making GitFile an even more user-friendly tool.

sections.text: Settlers of Solana Swarm of AI agents simulates a free-market economy on Solana. Inspiration Simulating an economy with artificial agents is not new: Salesforce's AI Economist did it with reinforcement learning. But an RL agent cannot tell you why it did anything, and cannot adapt when you change the rules. An LLM can. So we built the village we wanted, with production, price discovery and credit at once: agents that choose their own work, set their own prices, and can take out a collateralized loan, miss it, and be foreclosed on. AI agents are already paying each other for real, and about 65% of x402 payment volume settles on Solana. As more of finance runs on agents instead of people, being able to simulate how they behave matters more, and there is no reason to assume they behave like us. Furthermore, using Solana lets agents hold their own purses in a token no key can mint or freeze, including ours, so the rules are not ours to bend. Every round is on-chain for anyone to analyze. devpost_page.tagline: Inspired by Star Trek’s combadge and ship’s computer: a wearable AI communicator combining voice, vision, and actions. Just say, “Computer.”

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: We grew up watching Star Trek . As little kids, we saw the combadge and the ship’s computer as a futuristic, impossible innovation. How could a simple tap on the chest connect you to someone that could answer questions, do tasks, and act as your second brain? At Hack the North, we decided to bring that innovation to life.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Combadge has a chest-mounted touch sensor, LED, and haptic motor connected through conductive thread to a Raspberry Pi 5 on your belt. The Pi runs QNX 8.0 and connects to a microphone, speaker, and camera. You can talk naturally with Computer, ask it to look at something through the camera, search the live web, read or draft emails, manage calendar events, search for products, check Shopify inventory, prepare restock emails, and hand off a conversation to a real person by phone. For example, you could see something you like on a walk and say, “Computer, find me this under $50.” It'll take a snapshot through the camera (its eye) and try to find similar products on Shopify's platform.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We stitched conductive thread into the shirt to connect the chest-mounted badge to the Raspberry Pi at the waist. OpenAI GPT-Live powers the voice interface, while GPT-6 Astra handles reasoning and tool use. QNX runs the embedded system. Browserbase gives Computer access to the live web. Composio connects Gmail, Google Calendar, and Shopify. Shopify powers product discovery, checkout creation, and merchant inventory workflows.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text: One of the biggest challenges we faced was trying to get our Pi 5 to connect to our bluetooth speaker. QNX did not expose the bluetooth audio driver interfaces we needed. So we built our own path that sends generated PCM audio directly through our own Bluetooth driver . We also fixed a Python runtime issue that broke large TLS requests and made sure camera and network operations did not block live audio.

sections.heading: Accomplishments
sections.text: We are especially proud of turning the shirt itself into part of the circuit and building a Bluetooth audio path that our AI agents could help test physically. But most of all, the four of us got to see the futuristic innovation that amazed us come from the screen to life.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: We learned that making AI feel natural on real hardware is mostly an integration problem. Audio, networking, drivers, physical design, and interaction all matter. We also learned how useful an AI coding agent becomes when it can observe the physical result of its own work instead of only checking whether code ran successfully.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: It'd be great if we had a model to transform GPT-Live's voice into Majel Barrett-Roddenberry's, the voice actor for the Star Trek Combadge. We want to improve audio scheduling, echo cancellation, touch and haptic feedback, durability, comfort, and phone checkout handoff. Ultimately, we want to give you useful computing without pulling your attention away from the combat field that is the real world, just like the people in Star Trek.
